verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus:
Grace be to you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ:
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved.
In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace;
Wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence;
Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself:
That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him:
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ.
In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,
Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.
Wherefore I also, after I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints,
Cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers;
That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him:
The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power,
Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,
Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come:
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all.

chapters.summary: The letter opens with the plainest of addresses — "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus" — and then, with no news, no crisis, and no complaint to report, breaks straight into a single vast movement of praise. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ" fixes the terms of everything that follows: the blessing is already given rather than promised, it is spiritual rather than territorial, its location is "heavenly places," and every clause in the long sentence will fall back into the same refrain — in Christ, in him, in whom, in the beloved. Paul then traces the blessing backward past all history to its source, "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world," and immediately forward to its stated end, "that we should be holy and without blame before him in love," so that election is never an alternative to holiness but the appointed means of it. The choosing is filled out as adoption — "Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself" — and its motive is located nowhere in the chosen: "according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved." Only now, with the eternal decision named, does Paul touch the cross: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace," and grace is at once said to have overflowed "toward us in all wisdom and prudence," since what God gives includes the capacity to understand what he is doing. That understanding is then named a disclosed secret — "Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself" — and the content of the secret is the largest sentence in the letter: "That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him." The scope is cosmic, not merely personal; salvation is the reassembling of a fractured universe under one head. From that summit Paul descends to the readers' own experience in two movements marked by a shift of pronoun. First "we," those "who first trusted in Christ" and "have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will"; then "ye also," the Gentile hearers, whose entry is described as an ordinary sequence of hearing and believing — "after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise." The Spirit is called "the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession," a down payment on an estate not yet entered, and the whole outpouring closes as it began, "unto the praise of his glory." The second half of the chapter turns the doxology into intercession. Having heard of their "faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints," Paul does not cease "to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers," and what he asks for is not relief or increase but sight: that "the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: The eyes of your understanding being enlightened." Three things are to come into focus — "the hope of his calling," "the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints," and "the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe" — and the third is then measured against the only event adequate to it: that power is "according to the working of his mighty power, Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come." The chapter ends by attaching that enthroned Christ to a visible community: God "hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all."
takeaways: Everything in the opening blessing is spoken in the past tense of a completed act and in the locative case of a single person. God "hath blessed," "hath chosen," "having predestinated," "hath made us accepted," "hath abounded," "having made known" — and each verb terminates in Christ rather than in the believer considered by himself. This is why Paul can address a congregation about eternity without producing anxiety: the question is not whether an individual can locate his name on a hidden list, but whether he is in Christ, which is a question about a visible and enterable reality. The chapter never invites introspective auditing of one's own election; it invites praise, and it places the whole weight of assurance on the one in whom the choosing was made.

The purpose clauses are the discipline of the passage, and they are easy to skip. Election is "that we should be holy and without blame before him in love"; adoption is "To the praise of the glory of his grace"; the inheritance is "That we should be to the praise of his glory"; the sealing is "unto the praise of his glory." Paul states the doctrine three times and each time refuses to leave it as a bare fact about God's freedom, tethering it instead to an intended outcome in the chosen and a final outcome in God's own glory. A reading of predestination that produces either moral passivity or private complacency has severed the doctrine from the only ends the text assigns it.

Verse ten is the sentence the whole letter will spend six chapters unpacking: "That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth." The word behind "gather together in one" carries the sense of summing a column and writing the total at the head, and it presumes that the universe is currently in pieces. Redemption here is not primarily rescue of individuals out of a doomed world but the reunification of a divided one under a single head — which is why the ethical chapters will be preoccupied with walls broken down, walking worthy, and the knitting of a body. Personal salvation is real and assumed throughout, but it is presented as participation in something considerably larger than itself.

Paul describes the Ephesians' conversion with unglamorous ordinariness — "after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed" — and sets it directly beside the choosing made "before the foundation of the world." The two are not in competition; the eternal decision is executed in time through a preacher, a message, a hearing, and a believing. Whatever else predestination means in this chapter, it does not mean that preaching is decorative or that human response is fictional. The sealing that follows is described as ownership and guarantee at once, "the earnest of our inheritance," a first instalment that both proves the buyer's intent and is itself part of the sum.

The prayer of verses fifteen through nineteen asks for nothing the Ephesians do not already possess. Paul does not ask that they be given hope, an inheritance, or power; he asks that they may "know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, And what is the exceeding greatness of his power." The deficit he assumes in a healthy, believing congregation is a deficit of perception, and the remedy he asks for is not information but "the spirit of wisdom and revelation" and enlightened eyes. This is a distinctly unsentimental account of Christian growth: the chief thing lacking is the ability to see what is already true, and that ability is itself a gift to be prayed for rather than a skill to be acquired.

The chapter's final clause refuses to leave Christ's exaltation in the abstract. He is raised, seated, and set "Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion" — and then, immediately, "gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all." The cosmic sovereignty is given as a gift to a particular community, and the community is described not as his organisation or his audience but as his body and his fulness. Two consequences follow that the rest of the letter will press: the Church's life is not a human project supplemented by divine help, and the powers Paul names are not defeated somewhere else while the congregation waits, since the one seated above them is the same one whose body the congregation is.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:29-30 — whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son
crossRefs.why: This is the closest parallel in the letters to the chain of verbs in Ephesians 1, and it supplies both the same vocabulary of foreknowing and predestinating and the same insistence that the goal is conformity to Christ rather than bare selection. Read together the two passages check each other: Romans states the terminus as being "conformed to the image of his Son" and "the firstborn among many brethren," while Ephesians states it as holiness "before him in love" and adoption. Romans also draws the pastoral conclusion Ephesians leaves implicit, that the purpose of the doctrine is confidence under affliction — nothing "shall be able to separate us from the love of God" — which is why Paul can move from eternal decree to prison without embarrassment in both letters.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 1:16-20 — by him all things consist, and by him to reconcile all things unto himself
crossRefs.why: Colossians runs the same argument with the same peculiar breadth, reconciling "all things unto himself... whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven," and it makes explicit the point Ephesians compresses into "gather together in one all things in Christ." It also anticipates the last clause of this chapter, since it names Christ "the head of the body, the church" and says "it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell," the very word Ephesians applies to the Church as "the fulness of him that filleth all in all." Placing them side by side clarifies that the cosmic and the ecclesial claims in Ephesians are one claim and not two.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 7:7-8 — the LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number
crossRefs.why: Israel's election is the grammar Paul is speaking, and Deuteronomy states the logic he assumes: the choice is not explained by anything in the chosen, only by love and by an oath. It also matches Ephesians in refusing to let election terminate in privilege, since the next breath binds the chosen people to keep the commandments. Hearing this behind "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world" prevents the modern habit of treating predestination as an abstract puzzle about individual destinies; in its native setting it is covenant language about a people constituted by God's initiative and answerable for holiness.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 110:1 — Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool
crossRefs.why: Verses twenty through twenty-two are a mosaic of enthronement language, and this psalm is its principal source: the seating at the right hand and the placing of enemies under the feet are quoted rather than invented. Recognising the citation changes the register of Paul's prayer, since he is not offering a devotional image of Christ's glory but claiming that a specific royal oracle has been executed in the resurrection. It also explains why the list of defeated authorities is so long and so formal — "all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named" — because a coronation text requires an inventory of what has been subdued.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 1:22 — who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts
crossRefs.why: Paul uses the identical pair of images, sealing and earnest, in another letter and to a different end, which helps fix their meaning here. The seal marks ownership and authenticity; the earnest is a legally binding first instalment that guarantees the rest. In Corinth the point is the reliability of God's promises against a charge of fickleness — "all the promises of God in him are yea" — and that background sharpens "the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession" into a statement about God's own trustworthiness rather than about the believer's feelings.

crossRefs.label: John 6:37,44 — all that the Father giveth me shall come to me; no man can come to me, except the Father draw him
crossRefs.why: The Fourth Gospel places the same two claims in the same breath that Ephesians holds together: a prior divine giving and drawing, and a real coming that the person actually performs. Jesus can say both "no man can come to me, except the Father draw him" and "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out," which is precisely the structure of Ephesians 1, where choosing before the foundation of the world stands beside "after that ye heard... after that ye believed." Reading them together resists the temptation to resolve the tension by deleting one side of it.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:33 — being by the right hand of God exalted, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear
crossRefs.why: The first Christian sermon makes the same connection Ephesians makes between the enthronement and the gift of the Spirit: Christ is exalted, receives the promise of the Father, and pours it out on the hearers. That sequence explains why Paul can move without a seam from the sealing "with that holy Spirit of promise" in verse thirteen to the raising and seating of Christ in verse twenty — they are two ends of one event. It also grounds the abstract "heavenly places" of Ephesians in a datable public claim about a man raised from the dead.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world" and "having predestinated us unto the adoption of children... according to the good pleasure of his will," Catholic interpretation insists on the full force of the eternal decree while denying that it cancels genuine human freedom or that it includes a positive decree consigning anyone to ruin. The choosing is made "in him," so Christ is not merely the instrument of a prior selection but the very ground and pattern of it; predestination is read as God's eternal ordering of the elect to glory through grace that truly moves the will without violating it, since God's causality operates at a different level than creaturely causality and therefore does not compete with it. The passage is also read as speaking primarily of the Church as a body chosen in Christ rather than as a roster of isolated individuals whose destinies were settled apart from any means. Grace is prevenient, sovereign, and unearned, and the same grace produces a free consent that is genuinely the person's own; damnation, where it occurs, is permitted in view of foreseen resistance and is never symmetrical with election.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters read the passage as unconditional election in the strongest sense: the phrase "according to the good pleasure of his will" and the later "the counsel of his own will" are taken to exclude any foreseen faith or merit as the ground of choice, and the repeated "to the praise of the glory of his grace" is read as the deliberate closing of every door through which human contribution might enter. On this view God's choice is effectual, not merely enabling, and the will is not left finally undetermined; grace is irresistible in the sense that it certainly accomplishes what God intends. Many press that the pronouns are personal — "us," "we," "ye" — and resist reducing the election to a corporate category that anyone might join or leave. Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants, by contrast, stand closer to the Catholic account, reading the choosing as made in Christ and applied to those who by grace-enabled faith are found in him. All sides agree that the initiative is entirely God's, that no one is chosen for merit, and that the stated purpose of the decree is holiness and praise rather than speculation.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance" as language that the Church has always heard in a sacramental key. The seal is a real mark conferred, not merely a metaphor for an inward persuasion, and the tradition connects it with the anointing and the laying on of hands that complete Christian initiation, in which the Spirit given at baptism is confirmed and sealed. The "earnest" is understood as a genuine first instalment of glory already infused rather than only a promise about the future, which is why the tradition can speak of grace as truly possessed and lost, and of the Christian as really changed rather than only reckoned. Because the seal is a gift given in the visible order through the Church's ministry, assurance rests on the objectivity of what was done to the believer rather than on the intensity of his inner experience.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the sealing as coincident with believing — the text says "after that ye believed, ye were sealed" — and read it as the Spirit's own indwelling given to every believer without remainder, not as a further rite conferring something the believer lacked. Many treat the seal and the earnest together as the primary biblical basis for assurance and for the perseverance of the saints: a down payment that God does not forfeit guarantees the whole inheritance, so the sealed cannot finally be lost. Evangelical readers often add that the accent falls on divine ownership and protection rather than on any change of status mediated by an institution. Both traditions agree that the Spirit is given, that his presence is a pledge of a future not yet possessed, and that the guarantee rests on God's action rather than on the believer's constancy.

interpretationNotes.claim: The chapter's final clause — Christ "gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all" — is read in Catholic tradition as a statement about a visible, structured, historically continuous communion rather than about an invisible aggregate of the saved. If the Church is Christ's body and his fulness, then she is not an optional association of believers who already possess salvation individually but the very place where the gathering up of "all things in Christ" is happening in advance. This underwrites the conviction that the Church's unity is not merely spiritual and future but visible and required now, that her sacraments and ministry belong to her constitution as body rather than to her organisation as society, and that being joined to Christ and being joined to the Church are not two separable acts.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same high language while ordinarily distinguishing the one true Church, known certainly only to God and comprising all the elect in every age and place, from the visible congregations in which it is manifested and which can err. On this reading "his body" names a spiritual union created by the Spirit and faith, so that no single institution can identify itself simply with the referent, and the marks of a true church are located in the faithful preaching of the word and right administration of the sacraments rather than in institutional continuity. Many also stress that headship here is Christ's alone and cosmic in scope, cautioning against any construction in which a human office mediates that headship. Both traditions read the verse as forbidding a Christianity conceived without the Church, and both take "the fulness of him that filleth all in all" as an astonishing dignity conferred rather than achieved.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.

verses.text: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us,
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:
That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands;
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:
And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh.
For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord:
In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

chapters.summary: The chapter begins in the middle of a sentence whose main verb will not arrive for three verses, and the delay is the point. "And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins" states the diagnosis first: not sick, not weakened, not badly instructed, but dead. Paul then describes the condition as a way of walking rather than a mere status — "ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" — so that the death is simultaneously a captivity to an age, to a personal power, and to one's own appetites. Lest the Gentile readers hear this as an indictment of somebody else, Paul folds himself and his own people into it: "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others." The word "all" and the phrase "by nature" close every exit. Into that dead level ground drops the great adversative of the letter: "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ." Three compound verbs follow, all of them shared with Christ and all in the past tense — quickened together, "hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus" — so that the believer's biography is narrated as a participation in the resurrection and enthronement already described in the first chapter. The purpose is display over an unlimited horizon: "That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus." Then comes the sentence that has carried more theological freight than any other in the letter: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." Paul immediately supplies the balancing clause that is too often left off: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Works are excluded as the cause and reinstated as the purpose, and the same verb of walking that described the old captivity now describes the new life. The second half of the chapter takes the vertical rescue and lays it on its side. "Wherefore remember" — Paul commands memory, and what is to be remembered is a social and religious exclusion: "ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision," and worse, "at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world." Five deprivations, ending with the bleakest phrase in the letter. Against them stands one reversal: "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ." Paul then presses the peace between Jew and Gentile back into the person of Christ himself — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances" — and states the constructive purpose twice, "for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace" and "that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby." Reconciliation with God and reconciliation between enemies are accomplished in a single act and cannot be separated. Christ then "came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh," and the result is stated in the most Trinitarian sentence of the chapter: "For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father." The closing images pile up citizenship, family, and temple. They are "no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone," a structure that is not static but alive — "all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" — and whose purpose is habitation: "In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit."
takeaways: Paul's account of the human predicament is triple and refuses to settle on a single villain. The old walk was "according to the course of this world," an ambient current of the age; "according to the prince of the power of the air," a personal and hostile intelligence; and "in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind," a corruption running inward through appetite and thought alike. Blaming culture alone produces victims, blaming the devil alone produces excuses, and blaming appetite alone produces moralism. Holding all three explains why the remedy has to be resurrection rather than reform: a dead man is not improved by a better environment, a rescued hostage, or stronger resolve.

The three compound verbs of verses five and six — quickened together, raised up together, made to sit together — put the believer's present position inside an event that has already happened to someone else. Chapter one described God's power as that "Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places"; chapter two says the same three things about the Ephesians. This is why the letter can move so freely between cosmic language and pastoral advice, and why it never treats Christian ethics as an attempt to climb toward a status not yet held. The sitting is the strangest of the three and the most consequential: a seated person is neither anxious nor still striving for position.

Verses eight through ten form one argument and are habitually quoted as two. "By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast" is immediately grounded by "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." The Greek word rendered "workmanship" means something made, so the same sentence that denies human making affirms divine making, and the works excluded at the door reappear as the very floor the house is built on. The one thing the passage will not permit is boasting; it neither permits a Christianity that earns its standing nor one that has nothing to walk in once standing is given.

"Wherefore remember" is an imperative aimed at a specific amnesia. The Gentile converts are ordered to keep in mind that they were the outsiders, called "Uncircumcision" by others, "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise." Paul is not indulging in nostalgia for guilt; he is preventing the newly included from forgetting that they were included, which is the root of every subsequent contempt for those still outside and of every fantasy that one's place was always deserved. The phrase "having no hope, and without God in the world" also refuses a sentimental view of pre-Christian religion — the ancient world was crowded with gods, and Paul still calls it godless.

The peace of this chapter is not an attitude but a demolition. "He is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition" — peace is identified with a person and enacted by removing a barrier, and it costs the abolishing "in his flesh" of "the law of commandments contained in ordinances." What Paul sets aside is precisely the machinery of separation, the ceremonial and ritual boundary markers that made Jew and Gentile two peoples; he does not thereby set aside the moral demand, since he will spend chapters four through six issuing commands. The goal is stated constructively rather than merely negatively: not the assimilation of one group into the other, but the creation "in himself of twain one new man," a third thing that did not exist before.

The chapter ends with three images that correct one another. Citizenship answers the political exclusion of the aliens; household answers the loneliness of the strangers; temple answers the religious exclusion of those barred from the sanctuary. The temple image is the most demanding, because it is under construction and growing — "all the building fitly framed together groweth" — and because its purpose is not the accommodation of worshippers but the housing of God: "builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit." Individual Christians are not each a small temple in this passage; they are stones whose whole significance lies in being fitted to others, which makes disunity not a failure of manners but a structural defect in the dwelling God intends to occupy.

crossRefs.label: Romans 3:24,28 — being justified freely by his grace... a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law
crossRefs.why: Romans supplies the fuller forensic argument that Ephesians states as a settled conclusion, and it clarifies what Paul means when he excludes works. There the works in view are explicitly "the deeds of the law," and the immediate purpose of excluding them is to place Jew and Gentile on identical footing — "Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles?" — which is exactly the use Ephesians 2 makes of the same denial when it moves from grace to the broken wall. Reading them together shows that the exclusion of boasting is not merely about individual humility but about the impossibility of one people claiming advantage over another.

crossRefs.label: James 2:17,24 — faith, if it hath not works, is dead... by works a man is justified, and not by faith only
crossRefs.why: No text presses harder on the reading of Ephesians 2:8-9, and the two passages have to be held together rather than played off. James attacks a faith that is merely notional and produces nothing, insisting that such a faith is dead; Paul attacks a confidence in works that produces boasting, insisting that salvation is a gift. Ephesians itself supplies much of the reconciliation in verse ten, where the saved are "created in Christ Jesus unto good works," so that the works James demands as evidence are the works Paul says God prepared beforehand. The genuine disagreement between traditions is not about whether works follow but about how they relate to justification itself.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 2:13-14 — you, being dead in your sins... hath he quickened together with him, blotting out the handwriting of ordinances
crossRefs.why: The parallel is almost verbal: dead in sins, quickened together with him, and the cancelling of ordinances that stood against us. Colossians adds the image of the record nailed to the cross and the triumph over principalities, which supplies the missing middle term between the two halves of Ephesians 2 — the same cross that raises the dead also removes the legal apparatus of separation. Read side by side, the passages show that Paul thought of the abolition of the ceremonial boundary and the forgiveness of sins as one transaction rather than two.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 57:19 — Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the LORD
crossRefs.why: Verse seventeen is a quotation, and knowing it changes the sense of "came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh." The prophet's oracle promises peace across a distance God himself will bridge, and pairs it with the promise to dwell with the contrite. Paul takes the two distances of the oracle and identifies them with Gentile and Jew, so that a text about God's healing of his own people is stretched to cover the nations. The prophetic background also explains why he can say Christ "came and preached" peace when the risen Christ preached to Ephesus through apostles: the peace is proclaimed by the one who made it.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:28 — there is neither Jew nor Greek... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus
crossRefs.why: Galatians argues at length the point Ephesians assumes, that the law functioned as a custodian for a limited period and that its boundary-keeping role ends with the coming of faith. The resulting oneness is described in the same terms of a single new humanity, and the ground is baptismal incorporation — "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." That helps explain how Ephesians can pass so quickly from the abolition of ordinances to "one new man," and it locates the unity not in a shared opinion or a negotiated tolerance but in a common clothing with Christ.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 2:5-6 — ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house... a chief corner stone, elect, precious
crossRefs.why: Peter develops the same architecture with the same cornerstone, and adds two elements that fill out the Ephesian picture: the stones are living and are simultaneously the priesthood that serves in the house they compose. He also draws on the same prophetic stone oracles that stand behind Paul's "chief corner stone." The conjunction of temple and priesthood clarifies why Ephesians insists on access — "through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father" — since a temple without admitted worshippers would be a monument rather than a habitation.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 37:5,14 — I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live... and shall put my spirit in you
crossRefs.why: Ezekiel's valley supplies the governing image for the chapter's opening: a field of the unmistakably dead, incapable of contributing anything to their own revival, raised by a word and a breath. The vision also joins resurrection to reunification, since the next oracle takes two sticks and makes them "one stick" and one nation, which is precisely the movement from "quickened us together" to "of twain one new man." Ezekiel ends where Ephesians 2 ends, with God's sanctuary set in the midst of his people for ever, so the whole arc from death to indwelling temple is already sketched in the prophet.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast," Catholic interpretation affirms every clause without reservation and reads it as the definitive exclusion of any human initiative in salvation: the whole movement begins with unmerited grace, faith itself is a gift, and no one can place God in his debt. The tradition ordinarily takes the works excluded here in the sense the surrounding argument requires — deeds performed apart from grace, and in this letter especially the boundary-marking observances that let one group boast over another — since the very next verse describes the saved as "created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Because grace really transforms rather than merely covers, the good works that follow are genuinely the believer's own acts and are genuinely pleasing to God, so that the tradition can speak of merit while insisting that all such merit is itself God's gift crowning his own prior work. Justification is thus received freely and lived out really, and faith is understood as the beginning and root of a justification that includes love, since a faith severed from charity is not the living faith Paul has in view.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read this as the clearest statement in Scripture of justification by faith alone, and press the exclusion further: the works denied are not merely ceremonial or pre-conversion works but any works whatever considered as ground of acceptance, since the stated reason is the elimination of boasting as such rather than of one group's boast over another. On this view faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness accomplished entirely outside the believer and reckoned to him, and any language of merit — even merit described as God crowning his own gifts — reintroduces the very confidence the verse forbids. Verse ten is taken as decisive evidence that good works are the necessary fruit and proof of salvation rather than any part of its cause, and the phrase "before ordained that we should walk in them" is read as making even the believer's obedience a prepared gift. Both traditions confess that salvation originates wholly in grace, that faith is not a human achievement, that no one may boast, and that a life without good works contradicts the gospel it claims.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives full weight to "for to make in himself of twain one new man" and "reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross," hearing in it that the Church is not an association formed by reconciled individuals but the very form the reconciliation takes. Vertical peace with God and horizontal peace between former enemies are accomplished by one act and cannot be had separately, which is why visible communion — a single body with one altar and one shared life — belongs to the substance of the gospel rather than to its administration. The tradition draws from this the conviction that a division between Christian communities is not merely regrettable but is a wound in the thing Christ died to make, and that unity is therefore something to be restored and confessed rather than merely felt. The "one new man" language also rules out the reduction of the Church to either of its constituent peoples or to a federation of them.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same union while ordinarily locating it in the Spirit's work rather than in institutional form: the "one new man" is created by the cross and applied by faith, so that all who truly believe are already one body whether or not their congregations share governance. Many argue that this reading takes the passage more seriously, since the unity Paul describes is stated as an accomplished fact — "hath made both one" — and cannot be manufactured or forfeited by human organisation. Some also warn that identifying the one body too tightly with a visible structure risks the very boasting of insiders over outsiders that the passage was written to abolish. Both traditions agree that the peace is Christ's own achievement, that hostility between Christian groups contradicts the cross, and that the reconciliation is meant to be visible enough that watching outsiders can see it.

interpretationNotes.claim: The clause "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" is read in Catholic tradition as describing a real and continuing structure. The apostles are foundational not merely as the source of a message now preserved in writing but as the beginning of a ministry handed on, so that the Church's continuity with them is personal and institutional as well as doctrinal; the cornerstone remains Christ, who determines the alignment of every later stone, but the foundation course is genuinely laid by particular men whose office did not evaporate with them. The tradition also hears "prophets" here as the prophets of the new covenant named later in the letter alongside evangelists, pastors and teachers, so that the sentence describes the Church's ministerial constitution rather than the Old Testament canon. The building "fitly framed together" is accordingly not a metaphor for private believers each related separately to Christ, but for a fitted and ordered communion.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the foundation as the apostolic and prophetic testimony rather than the persons as officeholders — the Church is built on what the apostles taught, now inscribed in Scripture, which is why the foundation is by definition laid once and not repeatedly. On this account the cornerstone's primacy is emphatic and exclusive, and any structure claiming to continue the foundational office risks adding to a foundation the text presents as complete. Many take "prophets" as the Old Testament prophets precisely to make the point that Scripture in both testaments is the base on which the house stands. Both traditions agree that the Church did not invent itself, that it is answerable to the apostles rather than the reverse, and that Christ alone determines whether the whole building stands true.

verses.text: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,
If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward:
How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; ( as I wrote afore in few words,
Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ)
Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit;
That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel:
Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;
And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ:
To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,
According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:
In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him.
Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory.
For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named,
That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man;
That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,
May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;
And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.
Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

chapters.summary: Paul begins a prayer and does not finish it for thirteen verses. "For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" breaks off mid-thought, and the sentence is only resumed at verse fourteen with the same words, "For this cause I bow my knees." What interrupts is a digression about his own commission, and the interruption turns out to be necessary, because the readers cannot pray the prayer until they know why the man praying it is in chains. He describes his office as an administration entrusted rather than a career achieved — "the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward" — and its content as something he did not work out but received: "by revelation he made known unto me the mystery." The word mystery here means a secret now disclosed rather than a truth permanently obscure, and Paul is careful to say both that it "in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men" and that it "is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit," so the disclosure is neither private to him nor a novelty of his own devising. Then he states the secret in one line, and it is not what a religious imagination would predict: "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." The hidden purpose of the ages is a merger. Paul's own place in it is described with a superlative that outdoes ordinary modesty — "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given" — and the commission has two parts, to "preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" and "to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God." Verse ten then makes the most startling claim in the letter: the audience for this disclosure is not only human. "To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God" — the united Church is itself the exhibition, and the watching intelligences are the ones being instructed. This is said to be "According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord," and its practical fruit for the reader is immediate access: "In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him." Only then does Paul return to his chains, and he does so to protect his readers rather than himself: "Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory." The prayer resumes on his knees, addressed to "the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named," and it asks for a series of things that escalate past what a petition normally dares. First strength — "according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man" — then indwelling, "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith," then stability in love, "being rooted and grounded in love," the metaphors of a plant and a building set side by side. What all of this is for is comprehension, and the object is given only in dimensions without a noun: "May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height." Paul then names it and immediately concedes the impossibility: "And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge." The final clause asks for more than any of the preceding: "that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God." Aware that he has prayed past the edge of what can be requested, Paul closes not with amen but with a doxology that makes the excess into the point: "Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen."
takeaways: Paul's self-description controls the whole chapter. He is "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles," which reassigns the credit for his imprisonment away from Rome and toward Christ, and away from his own misfortune toward their benefit. He calls himself "less than the least of all saints" — a deliberately impossible comparative, as though the superlative were not low enough — and describes his commission as grace given rather than authority earned. The effect is that the most consequential ministry in the letter is presented as entirely derivative: a secret he did not deduce, an office he did not seek, a power he does not supply, and a suffering whose value belongs to somebody else.

The content of the mystery is the part most often blurred. Paul does not say the mystery is that God saves sinners, or that Christ died, or that grace is free; he says it is "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." Three compound words, each stressing togetherness, define the hidden purpose of the ages as the abolition of a religious frontier. That the epoch-making secret of God turns out to be the seating of former outsiders at the same table sets a permanent standard: any Christianity that quietly reinstates a first and second class of members has not merely failed at manners, it has obscured the specific thing God kept hidden for ages in order to reveal.

Verse ten reverses the expected direction of instruction. The Church is not primarily being taught here; she is the lesson — "that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God." The word rendered "manifold" suggests something many-coloured or intricately variegated, and what displays it is the improbable composition of a congregation containing people who had no business being in the same room. Angelic and hostile powers alike learn God's wisdom by observation of a mixed community, which means that reconciled diversity in the Church is not a social bonus attached to the gospel but part of its public demonstration in the unseen world.

The prayer of verses sixteen through nineteen is built as a sequence in which each request is the ground of the next, and the sequence moves from interior to immeasurable. Strength in "the inner man" makes room for Christ to "dwell in your hearts by faith"; indwelling produces rootedness "in love"; rootedness is what makes comprehension possible; comprehension terminates in knowing a love that "passeth knowledge"; and knowing that love ends in being "filled with all the fulness of God." Notably the comprehension is corporate — "with all saints" — so the dimensions cannot be measured alone. Paul assumes that the love of Christ is too large for any single Christian's perception and that the missing dimensions are held by other people.

The four dimensions are given without an object, and the omission is probably deliberate. "The breadth, and length, and depth, and height" names a magnitude in every direction without saying of what, and only the next clause supplies a candidate in "the love of Christ." The construction leaves the reader momentarily measuring nothing at all, which is the correct posture, and it is immediately followed by the admission that the thing measured "passeth knowledge." Paul is not being vague; he is asking for a knowledge that includes the recognition of its own insufficiency, a comprehension that grasps enough to know it has not grasped the whole. Devotion that claims to have taken the measure of Christ's love has misunderstood the prayer.

The doxology answers a problem the prayer itself created. Having asked for fulness with "all the fulness of God," Paul has requested something no petitioner can expect, and rather than retreat he escalates: God is "able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think." The measure of that ability is then located not in heaven but in the reader — "according to the power that worketh in us" — so that the same power that raised and seated Christ is named as already operative in an ordinary congregation. And the glory is directed to a specific address, "in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages," pairing the community and her Lord as the joint site where God's praise is rendered in time.

crossRefs.label: Acts 9:15 — he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles
crossRefs.why: The narrative of Paul's calling supplies the event behind his claim that "by revelation he made known unto me the mystery." Luke reports both the unsought nature of the encounter and the specific assignment to the nations, and adds the note that he would be shown "how great things he must suffer for my name," which explains why Paul can present his imprisonment as an ordinary feature of the commission rather than an interruption of it. The story also accounts for the extremity of "less than the least of all saints," since the man sent to the Gentiles had been on the road to arrest believers when he was stopped.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 1:26-27 — the mystery which hath been hid from ages... which is Christ in you, the hope of glory
crossRefs.why: Colossians uses the same vocabulary of a mystery hidden from ages and now made manifest, and states the Gentile dimension explicitly in "the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles." It also parallels the peculiar way Ephesians treats apostolic suffering as beneficial to the readers, since Paul there rejoices in his sufferings "for you" and speaks of filling up what remains of the afflictions of Christ for his body's sake. Reading the two together clarifies that "my tribulations for you, which is your glory" is not rhetorical flourish but a settled conviction about how apostolic hardship functions in the life of the churches.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 1:12 — which things the angels desire to look into
crossRefs.why: Peter offers the closest parallel to the strange claim of verse ten that angelic powers are the audience of the gospel's disclosure. There the prophets searched and the angels stoop to look at things now reported to the churches, so the drama of salvation is watched from outside human history. Set beside "might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God," it establishes that the New Testament writers thought of ordinary congregational life as observed by intelligences who are learning something from it — a perspective that raises the stakes of visible unity considerably above the level of institutional convenience.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 4:16 — let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace
crossRefs.why: Ephesians states almost without explanation that "we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him," and Hebrews supplies the reasoning: a high priest who has passed into the heavens and was tempted as we are makes approach both possible and unafraid. The pairing is useful because Ephesians derives access from the disclosure of the mystery and the reconciliation of the two peoples, while Hebrews derives it from priesthood and sacrifice; together they show that the same confidence is being argued from ecclesial and liturgical directions at once.

crossRefs.label: Romans 11:33 — O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments
crossRefs.why: Romans reaches the identical destination by a different road: a long argument about Jew and Gentile that ends in a doxology about unsearchable riches and wisdom, and even uses the word mystery for the arrangement by which the nations are brought in. The verbal overlap with "the unsearchable riches of Christ" and "the manifold wisdom of God" is close enough to suggest a settled pattern in Paul's thinking, in which reflection on the inclusion of the Gentiles reliably terminates in praise rather than in a system. It also supplies the note Ephesians assumes but does not state, that Israel's place in the arrangement is not abolished.

crossRefs.label: John 14:23 — we will come unto him, and make our abode with him
crossRefs.why: Paul prays "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith," and the promise in the upper room supplies the theology behind the request: the Father and the Son come and take up residence with the one who keeps Christ's word, and the Spirit is given as the agent of that presence. The parallel also explains the odd structure of the Ephesian prayer, in which the Spirit strengthens the inner man so that Christ may dwell there, since in John the indwelling is a joint and Trinitarian act rather than a series of separate visits.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 12:3 — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed
crossRefs.why: The promise to Abraham is the oldest form of the secret Paul says was "hid in God," and its presence in the text raises the question of what exactly was hidden. The nations' blessing was announced from the beginning; what was not disclosed was the manner — that they would be "fellowheirs, and of the same body," incorporated on equal terms rather than admitted as clients. Reading the promise behind the mystery keeps Paul's claim from sounding like a rupture with Israel's scriptures, and shows him arguing that the ancient covenant is being executed rather than replaced.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading fastens on the phrase "is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit" as evidence that revelation is given to and through a body of commissioned witnesses rather than to individuals reading in isolation. Paul insists that the mystery came to him by revelation, but he immediately places that revelation alongside what was given to the other apostles, so the criterion of authenticity is agreement with an apostolic company and not private certainty. The tradition draws from this the conviction that the deposit of revelation is entrusted to the Church and handed on within her living teaching, so that Scripture is read inside the community that received it rather than over against her. The chapter's climax reinforces this, since the wisdom of God is made known "by the church" — the community is the organ of the disclosure, not merely its beneficiary.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasise that Paul directs the readers to a written text as the check on his claims — "as I wrote afore in few words, Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ" — and take this as evidence that the apostolic message was from the outset committed to writing precisely so that ordinary hearers could verify it for themselves. On this reading the apostles and prophets are foundational and unrepeatable, and the mystery once revealed is now possessed in the apostolic writings rather than in a continuing office of disclosure. Many also note that the Church in verse ten displays God's wisdom to the powers rather than defining it. Both traditions agree that the revelation is not privately generated, that it came through the apostles, and that no later authority may add a new mystery to the one Paul says has been made known.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "my tribulations for you, which is your glory," Catholic interpretation reads apostolic suffering as genuinely fruitful for others rather than merely exemplary. Paul does not say his sufferings encourage them or illustrate a principle; he says the tribulations are for them and are their glory, which the tradition understands in terms of a real solidarity in the body whereby one member's affliction, joined to Christ's own passion, benefits the rest. This underwrites the Church's practice of offering suffering in union with Christ for the good of others and her conviction that the communion of saints involves an actual exchange of spiritual goods across the body. Nothing is added to the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice; what is affirmed is that his members are permitted to participate in its application in ways that genuinely help one another.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters typically read the verse in a more direct sense: Paul's imprisonment is their glory because it is the proof and price of the gospel having reached them, and because a suffering apostle vindicates rather than discredits the message. They resist any construction in which human suffering possesses redemptive value, insisting that Christ's passion is complete and unrepeatable and that believers benefit others by proclamation, service and prayer rather than by a transfer of merit. Many add that Paul's stated concern is pastoral — "that ye faint not" — so the sentence functions to steady readers who might read his chains as failure. Both traditions hold that suffering for the gospel is not wasted, that it belongs to apostolic ministry rather than contradicting it, and that Christ's own sacrifice needs no supplement.

interpretationNotes.claim: The prayer that the readers "might be filled with all the fulness of God" is read in Catholic tradition as language of real participation in the divine life, not merely of moral improvement or of a legal relation. Grace is understood to effect a genuine transformation of the person, so that the God who is comprehended in love actually indwells and communicates his own life, and the saints are made partakers of the divine nature without ceasing to be creatures. This underlies the tradition's confidence that sanctification is a real ontological change progressively worked out, that holiness is genuinely attainable by grace in this life, and that the beatific vision toward which the prayer strains is continuous with what is begun now. Verse twenty then guards the whole against presumption by locating the power in God, who does "exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the Spirit's real indwelling and progressive sanctification while ordinarily preferring relational and covenantal language to that of infused participation, and insisting that the believer's standing before God never rests on the degree of transformation achieved. Many read "filled with all the fulness of God" as a corporate prayer for the Church to be filled with God's presence and character, pointing to "with all saints" in the preceding verse, rather than as a description of individual ontological elevation. Some also stress that the prayer is asked, not reported, and remains eschatological in reach. Both traditions agree that the goal of Christian life is God himself rather than a benefit obtained from him, that the change worked in believers is genuine and not fictional, and that the whole is powered by God rather than achieved by effort.
