verses.text: I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called,
With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love;
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;
One Lord, one faith, one baptism,
One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.
But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ.
Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.
( Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth?
He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things.)
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind,
Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:
Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
But ye have not so learned Christ;
If so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus:
That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;
And be renewed in the spirit of your mind;
And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Neither give place to the devil.
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.

chapters.summary: The hinge of the letter falls at the first word: "I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you." Everything from here is consequence, and the man drawing the consequence has no leverage but his chains and his affection — he beseeches rather than commands. The single demand is that they "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called," and its first content is not doctrinal correctness or moral achievement but temperament: "With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." The verb is strenuous and the object is not manufactured — unity already exists as the Spirit's work, and what is asked is that it be kept. Paul then grounds the appeal in a list of seven singulars that reads like a creed cut to the bone: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." Having pressed oneness to the limit, he immediately turns to difference without apology: "But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ." The differences are distributions from a single source, and Paul proves it with a citation about a conquering king dividing spoil — "When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men" — pausing to insist that the ascent presupposes a descent, since "He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things." The gifts he then names are not abilities but persons: "he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers." Their purpose is stated in a three-fold phrase, "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ," and the horizon is corporate maturity: "Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ." The alternative is childhood in its least attractive form, believers "tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive." Against manipulation Paul sets the compound discipline of "speaking the truth in love," and describes growth as an organic operation in which every part contributes: "the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love." The second half turns to the walk itself. Paul "testifies in the Lord" that they must not walk "as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind," and traces the pagan condition through a chain of causes — darkened understanding, alienation "from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them," ignorance rooted in "the blindness of their heart" — ending in numbness: "Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness." Against this stands a curiously personal formula, "But ye have not so learned Christ," as though Christ were himself the curriculum, and the lesson learned is stated as a change of clothes: put off "the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts," "be renewed in the spirit of your mind," and put on "the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." The chapter closes with concrete instances, each with a reason attached. Lying is put away because "we are members one of another"; anger is permitted but time-limited — "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" — because delay gives ground to an enemy, "Neither give place to the devil"; the thief is not merely stopped but redirected into work "that he may have to give to him that needeth"; speech is regulated by its effect on hearers, "that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers." Then the sharpest motive in the list: "And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption" — the offended party in ordinary congregational unkindness is a person who can be grieved. Five hostile dispositions are to be carried out together, "all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking... with all malice," and three replacements installed in their place, with the pattern named last: "be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you."
takeaways: Paul asks the Ephesians to keep a unity rather than to build one, and the distinction governs the whole chapter. "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" assumes that the oneness is already a fact created by God — the seven singulars of verses four through six are indicative statements, not goals — and that the human work is custodial. This rules out two opposite errors: treating unity as a negotiable achievement that the sufficiently diplomatic might construct, and treating it as an invisible reality so secure that visible fractures do not matter. The virtues named as its means are all unglamorous and all relational — lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, forbearance — which locates the practical threat to unity in ordinary personal friction rather than in theological complexity.

The seven singulars are stacked in a deliberate order that moves outward and upward: one body and one Spirit, called in one hope; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all. The middle triad is the confession, the first triad is the community it creates, and the last is the source of both. That "one baptism" sits inside a creedal list of things as non-negotiable as the one Lord and the one God is significant, since it treats a sacramental act as constitutive of the Church's oneness rather than as a denominational preference. The closing phrase then refuses every attempt to keep God at one distance only: he is "above all, and through all, and in you all" — transcendent, pervasive, and indwelling in the same breath.

Verse eleven gives the Church offices rather than techniques, and verse twelve tells us what they are for in a phrase that has been read two ways with real consequences. "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ" either lists three parallel purposes of the ordained, or describes a chain in which leaders equip the saints so that the saints do the work of ministry and thereby build the body. The second reading is favoured by verse sixteen, where growth comes "by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part." Either way, the outcome is not a well-run institution but a body arriving "unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ," and the offices exist to make themselves less necessary rather than more.

The picture of immaturity is unexpectedly specific: not ignorance but instability, believers "tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine." What makes them vulnerable is not lack of intelligence but the presence of "sleight of men, and cunning craftiness" — Paul assumes the existence of skilled religious manipulators who lie in wait, and he assumes that doctrinal weather is a permanent feature of church life. The stated antidote is neither a stronger authority structure nor a hardening against all novelty, but "speaking the truth in love," a compound that resists both the loveless truth-teller who wounds and the loving evader who lets error stand. Maturity in this passage is measured by settledness under pressure and by growth into a head, not by the accumulation of information.

The transformation of verses twenty-two through twenty-four is described in a sequence that resists both moralism and passivity. The old man is put off, the mind is renewed, the new man is put on — an outer action, an inner alteration, and another outer action — and the new man is not constructed by the believer but is "after God... created in righteousness and true holiness." What the Christian does is dress in something already made. Behind the clothing image lies the phrase "ye have not so learned Christ," which treats a person rather than a code as the content of moral instruction; ethics here is not the application of principles but the wearing of a nature received.

Every command in the closing section carries a stated reason, and the reasons are almost all relational rather than abstract. Truth-telling rests on membership — "for we are members one of another" — so that lying is treated as a body attacking itself rather than as a violation of a rule. Work is reframed away from self-support toward provision for others, "that he may have to give to him that needeth," so that even the reformed thief is not merely made harmless but made useful. Speech is judged entirely by its effect on hearers, and the whole is placed under the warning "grieve not the holy Spirit of God," which makes the tone of congregational conversation a matter of personal offence to God rather than of etiquette. The final clause sets the standard and the resource in the same sentence: forgiveness is required "even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you," a measure no one can meet who has not first been on the receiving end of it.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 68:18 — Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men
crossRefs.why: This is the text Paul cites in verse eight, and the difference between the psalm and his quotation is the most discussed feature of the chapter. The psalm celebrates a victorious God ascending Zion and receiving tribute from the conquered; Paul has the ascended one giving gifts instead of receiving them. Whether he is drawing on a known interpretive rendering or making the shift deliberately, the effect is to portray Christ's ascension as a triumph whose spoil is distributed downward to his people rather than hoarded. Reading the psalm first also supplies the martial background that makes "he led captivity captive" a claim about defeated powers rather than a decorative phrase.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 — the body is one, and hath many members... ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular
crossRefs.why: Corinth receives the same doctrine applied to a congregation tearing itself apart over rank. Paul there insists on diversity of gifts from one Spirit, on the indispensability of the apparently weaker members, and on suffering and rejoicing shared across the whole. Ephesians compresses that argument into "that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part," and adds what Corinthians leaves implicit — a head toward which the body grows. Read together, the two passages show that the body image is used both to humble those who think themselves essential and to enlist those who think themselves negligible.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 3:9-10 — ye have put off the old man with his deeds; and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge
crossRefs.why: The parallel is close enough to function as a commentary: the same clothing metaphor, the same renewal, and the same catalogue of vices to be put off and virtues to be put on, ending in forgiveness patterned on Christ's. Colossians adds the crucial detail that in the new man "there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision," tying the ethical change directly to the abolition of the wall described in Ephesians 2. It also states the tenses more sharply, treating the putting off as already done, which helps clarify whether Ephesians is describing a completed act, a repeated discipline, or both.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 4:4 — Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still
crossRefs.why: Verse twenty-six is drawn from this psalm, and the original setting explains the otherwise puzzling permission to be angry. The psalmist addresses men who have wronged him, urging them to feel the weight of it, to reflect in silence at night, and to stop short of sin — anger is not forbidden but is put under a curfew and a discipline of self-examination. That background makes "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" less a rule about bedtime than a refusal to let a legitimate grievance harden overnight into a settled disposition, which is exactly the transition from the permitted anger of verse twenty-six to the forbidden bitterness of verse thirty-one.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 63:10 — they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy
crossRefs.why: Paul's warning "grieve not the holy Spirit of God" echoes a passage in which Israel's rebellion is said to have vexed the Spirit who carried them through the wilderness. The prophetic background gives the phrase its full weight: the Spirit is not an impersonal force to be quenched or a mood to be dampened, but a personal presence with a history of patient carrying who can be wounded by the conduct of the people he leads. It also sets the ordinary sins Paul is discussing — lying, bitterness, corrosive speech — on a continuum with covenant rebellion rather than treating them as minor congregational blemishes.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:32-33 — shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee
crossRefs.why: The parable dramatises the logic of the chapter's last verse, "forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you." The servant's failure is not primarily unkindness but incoherence: a man carrying an unpayable debt already cancelled cannot consistently pursue a trivial one. Its setting inside a discourse on how members of the community are to handle one another's sin makes it an unusually exact parallel to Ephesians 4, where the forgiveness commanded is specifically intramural. It also supplies the sober note Paul leaves unstated, that refusing to extend what one has received is a matter of judgment rather than of temperament.

crossRefs.label: John 17:21 — that they all may be one... that the world may believe that thou hast sent me
crossRefs.why: Christ's own prayer supplies the theological ground for Paul's plea and states the stake Ephesians leaves implicit. The oneness asked for is patterned on the union of Father and Son, given rather than negotiated, and it is explicitly evangelistic — the world's belief hangs on whether it is visible. That pairing sharpens the force of "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit," since what is at risk in congregational bitterness is not merely internal comfort but the credibility of the claim that the Father sent the Son.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "one body... one faith, one baptism" as a statement that the Church's unity is meant to be visible, doctrinal and sacramental at once, and not merely spiritual. The seven singulars are read as inseparable: one cannot hold the one Lord while treating the one body as an invisible abstraction, or hold the one baptism while regarding the shared confession as negotiable. The tradition draws from this both the seriousness with which it treats division — schism is not a difference of preference but a tearing of something Christ made one — and the conviction that unity has a definite content that can be identified and must be professed together, which is why creeds, the common celebration of the sacraments and communion with a recognised ministry are treated as expressions of this verse rather than additions to it. That baptism appears once and unrepeatably also grounds the tradition's practice of recognising a valid baptism performed outside her visible boundaries, since there is only one.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same seven singulars while ordinarily locating the unity in the Spirit's creation of one people out of all true believers, so that the "one body" is real and even visible in local congregations and shared confession without requiring a single institutional structure. Many argue that Paul commands the keeping of a unity that already exists precisely because it cannot be destroyed by human organisation, and that the marks by which the one Church is recognised are the gospel rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered rather than continuity of office. Baptist and free-church readers add that "one baptism" identifies the single rite of Christian initiation rather than authorising a particular mode or subject. Both traditions treat division as a scandal rather than a neutral diversity, and both read the verse as forbidding a Christianity in which believers are indifferent to their separation from one another.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints," Catholic interpretation reads a divinely given ministerial structure rather than a description of spontaneous congregational functions. The offices are Christ's own gift from his ascension, listed in a definite order, and given for the equipping of the whole body toward maturity, which grounds the conviction that ordained ministry belongs to the Church's constitution rather than to her convenience and that it is received from Christ rather than delegated upward by the congregation. The tradition also reads the passage as forbidding clericalism from the other direction, since the purpose clause makes the perfecting of the saints and the growth of the whole body the point of the offices, so that a ministry that produces passive members has failed at the task for which it was given.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters commonly divide the list into foundational and continuing gifts, taking apostles and prophets as belonging to the laying of the foundation described earlier in the letter and evangelists, pastors and teachers as ongoing, so the passage describes function more than a fixed hierarchy. Many press the punctuation of verse twelve hard, reading it as leaders equipping the saints to do the work of ministry, and treat this as the charter of the priesthood of all believers against any division of the Church into a ministering class and a receiving one. Charismatic and restorationist readers, by contrast, argue that all five continue. Both traditions agree that the ministries are given by the ascended Christ rather than self-assumed, that their measure of success is the maturity of the whole body, and that the congregation is never merely an audience.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears in "grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption" a real possibility that grace can be resisted, wounded and ultimately lost. The Spirit is a person who can be grieved, the seal is set with a view to a future day not yet reached, and the whole surrounding paragraph presumes that baptised believers may lie, nurse bitterness, steal and corrupt others — conduct the letter treats as genuinely dangerous rather than merely inconsistent. This grounds the tradition's account of mortal sin, of the need for ongoing repentance and sacramental reconciliation, and of perseverance as a gift to be prayed for rather than a possession to be presumed upon. The warning is read as pastoral realism rather than as a threat to assurance, since the same Spirit who can be grieved is the one who supplies the strength to obey.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters read the sealing "unto the day of redemption" as the strongest possible guarantee that the Spirit will not abandon those he has marked, and take the warning as one of the means God uses to keep his people rather than as evidence that they may be lost. On this account grieving the Spirit costs joy, fruitfulness and the sense of God's favour, but not the standing itself, since a seal that could be broken would be no guarantee. Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants stand much closer to the Catholic reading here, treating the warnings as genuine and apostasy as a real possibility. All sides agree that the verse assumes the Spirit is personal, that Christian conduct genuinely affects the relationship, and that the warning is addressed to real believers rather than to pretenders.

verses.text: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints;
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience.
Be not ye therefore partakers with them.
For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light:
( For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth;)
Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord.
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret.
But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light.
Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ;
Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.
Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.
For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.
Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word,
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.
For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church:
For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones.
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.

chapters.summary: The chapter opens with the most audacious imperative in the letter, stated as though it were obvious: "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children." Imitation of God is made possible only by the family relation that precedes it, and its content is immediately narrowed to one thing — "walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour." The pattern to be imitated is a self-donation described in the vocabulary of the altar, so love here is defined by a death rather than by an emotion. What follows is the negative image of that love, and Paul sets three vices side by side that the ancient world would not have grouped together: "fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints." Sexual disorder and greed belong to the same family because both take rather than give. The regulation extends past conduct to speech — "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient" — and the prescribed replacement is not solemnity but gratitude, "but rather giving of thanks," since thanksgiving is the speech of a person who has received rather than seized. Then a hard warning: "no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God," with covetousness explicitly named idolatry, and a caution against those who will soften it — "Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience." Paul then reaches for the image that governs the middle of the chapter, and states it as identity rather than aspiration: "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" — not in darkness and in light, but darkness and light. The command follows the fact: "walk as children of light," bearing "the fruit of the Spirit... in all goodness and righteousness and truth," and "Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord." The relation to surrounding corruption is neither participation nor silence: "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them," a reproof that works by exposure, since "all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light." The section closes with what sounds like a fragment of an early baptismal hymn: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light." From there the tone becomes practical and urgent — "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" — with wisdom defined not as insight in general but as "understanding what the will of the Lord is." The contrast that follows is the chapter's structural pivot: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." Both are conditions in which a person is governed by something outside himself, and Paul specifies what Spirit-filling looks like in a series of participles that are all corporate and vocal: "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God." That last participle carries directly into the household instructions, so mutual submission is presented as the fourth mark of a Spirit-filled congregation rather than as a new subject. "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord" is grounded in a headship immediately qualified by rescue — "the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body." The husband's command is longer and costlier: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it," and the purpose clauses describe not the husband's benefit but the beloved's transformation, "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish." Paul then argues from bodily self-interest — "He that loveth his wife loveth himself. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones" — and quotes the founding text of marriage, "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh." The comment that follows is the most consequential sentence in the chapter: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." Then, having ascended to the union of Christ and his body, Paul comes back down to the room: "Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband."
takeaways: Paul groups fornication, uncleanness and covetousness as a single category and then calls the third of them idolatry, which is a more radical claim than it appears. What binds them is acquisition: each treats another person or thing as material for one's own satisfaction, and each is therefore the exact inverse of the love just defined as Christ "hath given himself for us." The chapter's ethics of sex and its ethics of money are not two topics but one, and both are measured against a self-donation. Naming greed as idolatry also removes the comfortable distinction by which a respectable congregation deplores sexual sin while treating acquisitiveness as ambition, since the letter puts them under the same verdict about inheritance in the kingdom.

The command about speech is easy to misread as prudishness. "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" is not a prohibition on humour but on a particular use of speech — the corrosive, knowing, degrading wit that makes other people material for amusement — and the alternative offered is not silence or gravity but thanksgiving. That substitution is precise: the person whose habitual speech is gratitude has already conceded that he is a recipient, which is the disposition that makes both greed and contempt impossible. Read alongside the previous chapter's rule that speech should "minister grace unto the hearers," Paul is treating a community's ordinary conversation as one of its principal spiritual disciplines.

"Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" states the change as a change of substance rather than of location or behaviour, and the imperative follows rather than produces it. This ordering is consistent across the letter and governs how the ethical chapters should be heard: the commands never construct an identity, they express one already conferred. The consequence for engagement with a corrupt world is equally carefully balanced — "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them" — which is neither participation nor withdrawal but exposure. The mechanism is stated as almost passive: light does not argue, it makes things visible, so the first form of Christian reproof is the presence of a community whose ordinary life shows what the alternative actually costs.

"Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" sets two states of being governed against each other, and the comparison is more exact than it is flattering. Both involve a person acting under an influence he has admitted, and both alter speech and inhibition. The difference lies in what the influence produces: dissipation and loss of self on one side, and on the other four participles that are all outward-facing — singing to one another, praise directed to the Lord, thanksgiving "always for all things," and mutual submission. Notably Paul defines Spirit-filling almost entirely in terms of what a congregation does together, not by private experience, and includes yielding to other people as one of its constituent marks.

The household instructions begin under the heading of verse twenty-one, "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God," and the grammar of verse twenty-two depends on it, since the Greek supplies no second verb for the wives. That structure means the specific submissions that follow are instances of a mutuality that binds everyone, not exceptions to it, and it sets the frame in which the asymmetry of the commands must be read. The asymmetry is real and should not be smoothed away: wives are told to submit, husbands are not told to submit in the same words. But the husband's assignment is by far the heavier, since it is defined by the cross rather than by authority, and its stated aim is his wife's holiness rather than his own convenience — a headship measured entirely by what it gives up.

The sequence at the end moves in an unexpected direction. One would expect Paul to explain the union of Christ and the Church by appealing to marriage as an illustration; instead he treats the union of Christ and the Church as the reality and marriage as the thing that has been pointing to it since Eden. "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" claims that the one-flesh clause of the creation account was always about more than a household. This inverts the usual order of explanation and gives ordinary marriage a weight it cannot carry on its own terms: it is a sign of something, and its obligations follow from what it signifies. The final verse then prevents the whole discussion from floating off into symbolism, returning to a particular man, a particular wife, and the daily work of love and reverence.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:24 — therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this verse and then says he is speaking of Christ and the Church, so the creation account is not decoration but the load-bearing text of his argument. In Genesis the one-flesh clause is the narrator's conclusion drawn from the woman being taken from the man's side, which explains Paul's otherwise odd phrase "members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones" — he is reading the Church as formed from Christ in the way Eve was formed from Adam. Reading the original also establishes that marriage was instituted before the fall and carries a meaning independent of it, which is why Paul can treat it as a sign rather than a concession.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 3:16-19 — let the word of Christ dwell in you richly... wives, submit yourselves; husbands, love your wives
crossRefs.why: The parallel passage runs the identical sequence — indwelling, psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, thanksgiving, then household instructions — but substitutes "let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" where Ephesians has "be filled with the Spirit," which is a useful check on both. It also states the husband's command with a warning attached, "and be not bitter against them," and gives the wife's submission a limiting qualifier, "as it is fit in the Lord." The compression in Colossians makes clear that Ephesians is expanding a shared pattern of instruction rather than inventing an argument for one congregation's local problem.

crossRefs.label: Hosea 2:19-20 — I will betroth thee unto me for ever... in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness
crossRefs.why: The prophetic tradition of God as husband to an unfaithful people is the background against which Paul's marriage analogy has to be heard. Hosea's God does not merely command fidelity but woos, purifies and betroths a bride who has already broken the covenant, which supplies the note of rescue in "he is the saviour of the body" and the purpose of cleansing in "that he might sanctify and cleanse it." The prophet also shows that the marriage image is not primarily about hierarchy but about covenant loyalty and the restoration of a ruined relationship, which shifts the centre of gravity in Ephesians 5 from authority to faithfulness.

crossRefs.label: Revelation 19:7-8 — the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready
crossRefs.why: Paul says Christ will "present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle," and the vision of the marriage supper supplies the scene toward which that presentation moves. The bride there is arrayed in fine linen explicitly identified as the righteousness of saints, which holds together the two things Ephesians asserts at once — that the cleansing is Christ's work and that the resulting holiness is genuinely the Church's own. Reading them together also makes clear that the chapter's marriage language is eschatological: the husband's love images something that has not yet reached its completion.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 60:1 — Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee
crossRefs.why: Verse fourteen's "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light" is introduced with a formula of citation but matches no single scripture exactly, and this oracle is among the texts whose language it gathers — a summons to rise, a light arriving from outside, and a people who were in darkness. The prophetic setting, where the light on Zion draws the nations to her brightness, matches the movement of Ephesians from Gentile darkness to inclusion in the one body. It also explains why the summons is addressed to those already in covenant: the call to awake is not evangelistic recruitment but the rousing of a people who possess a light they are not yet walking in.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:3-8 — in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves... he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death
crossRefs.why: The letter to Philippi supplies the fullest statement of the logic underlying "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" and the husband's command to love as Christ loved. There the mutual deference of a congregation is grounded in a descent from equality with God to the death of a slave, and the same descent is presented as the mind Christians are to have among themselves. Set beside Ephesians 5, it establishes that headship exercised as self-expenditure is not a softening of the concept but its Christian definition, and that mutual submission is a doctrine about Christ before it is a rule about households.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 6:9-10,16 — the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God... he which is joined to an harlot is one body
crossRefs.why: Corinth receives the same list of excluded conduct and the same conclusion about inheriting the kingdom, and it makes explicit what Ephesians assumes about why sexual sin is treated with such gravity. Paul there quotes the identical one-flesh clause from Genesis to argue that bodily union is never merely physical, and grounds the whole appeal in the body being a temple of the Holy Spirit. Read together, the passages show that the marriage theology of Ephesians 5 and the sexual ethics of its opening verses rest on one conviction, that union of bodies signifies and effects something real.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church," Catholic interpretation reads marriage as a sacrament in the proper sense: a sign instituted by Christ that not only represents the union of Christ and the Church but actually confers the grace it signifies. The word rendered "mystery" is the term that early Latin tradition translated as sacrament, and the passage is understood to mean that the one-flesh union established at creation was always ordered toward the union of Christ with his body, so that a Christian marriage participates in that union rather than merely illustrating it. From this follows the tradition's insistence on the indissolubility of a consummated sacramental marriage — since Christ does not abandon his Church, the sign cannot be dissolved without falsifying what it signifies — and its treatment of the spouses' mutual self-gift as a genuine means of sanctification. The purpose clauses of verses twenty-six and twenty-seven are also read as language of baptismal washing, so the chapter joins the sacrament that makes the Church to the sacrament that images her.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally hold that the word here means a previously hidden truth now revealed, as it plainly does earlier in this same letter, and that translating it as sacrament imports a later category the text does not carry. On this reading marriage is a creation ordinance and a divinely honoured estate rather than a sacrament, since the two rites the Reformers retained were those they judged to have been instituted by Christ with a promise of grace attached, and marriage predates the gospel and is shared with unbelievers. Most therefore read the analogy as profoundly instructive without conferring grace, and while regarding divorce as a grave evil, allow that Christ's own exception and the case of desertion admit dissolution in limited circumstances. Both traditions read the passage as making marriage far more than a contract, as grounding its obligations in Christ's own fidelity, and as forbidding the treatment of a spouse as a possession.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" as the governing principle of the whole household section and reads the subsequent asymmetry within it rather than against it. Headship is understood as a real ordering within a communion of equal persons, not a difference of dignity, and it is defined by the model given — a head who "gave himself for it" and whose authority is exercised entirely as self-expenditure for the other's holiness. The tradition therefore reads the husband's command as by far the more demanding and reads the wife's submission as freely given within a mutual gift, while insisting that no reading which produces domination or reduces the wife to an instrument can be faithful to a text whose stated pattern is the cross. That the passage sits inside a discussion of Spirit-filling further indicates that these relations are meant to be lived as grace rather than enforced as law.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers divide sharply here. Complementarian interpreters argue that verse twenty-one describes submission within appropriate relations rather than an undifferentiated mutuality, and that a distinct male headship in the home is taught by the analogy itself, since the Church does not exercise headship over Christ. Egalitarian interpreters press the grammar of verse twenty-two, which borrows its verb from verse twenty-one, and read the household instructions as a subversion of the ancient household codes from within — each subordinate party is addressed as a moral agent and each dominant party is given the harder command. Both Protestant camps agree with the Catholic reading that the husband's love is defined by Christ's self-giving, that headship in this passage never authorises coercion, and that the wife is addressed as a person capable of her own free obedience to the Lord.

interpretationNotes.claim: The clause "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" is read in Catholic tradition as a direct reference to baptism, and as evidence that the sacrament genuinely effects what it signifies. The washing is not said to picture cleansing but to accomplish it, the agent is Christ, and the instrument is water joined to the word — a formula the tradition reads as the pattern of sacramental action generally, in which a material sign and the word of Christ together convey grace. Because the object cleansed is the Church rather than an individual, the verse also grounds the conviction that baptism incorporates a person into a body rather than merely settling a private transaction, which is why the letter can move from washing to the presentation of a whole glorious Church without spot or wrinkle.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that baptism is in view but locate the effective agent in the word rather than the water, noting that Paul specifies "by the word" and reading the washing as the sign and seal of a cleansing accomplished by Christ's blood and received by faith. Reformed and Lutheran readers differ among themselves about how closely the sign and the thing signified are joined, with Lutherans holding a genuinely instrumental view close to the Catholic one; Baptist readers stress that the washing follows faith and signifies a cleansing already granted. Many also emphasise that the whole sentence is about Christ's action on the Church and warn against any reading that transfers the efficacy to the minister or the rite considered by itself. Both traditions confess that the cleansing is Christ's work, that it is corporate as well as personal, and that it is aimed at a holiness to be completed at his presentation of the Church to himself.

verses.text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
Honour thy father and mother; ( which is the first commandment with promise;)
That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth.
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ;
Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart;
With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men:
Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free.
And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.
Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness;
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;
And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel,
For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.
But that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things:
Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that ye might know our affairs, and that he might comfort your hearts.
Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity. Amen.
